    Track 1 · SFT fundamentals · Lesson 18

    Evaluation that matches the task

    After this lesson you can design an evaluation for your task: pick a shape-appropriate metric, run it on the gold set against a baseline, set a pass gate, and report results honestly.

    Level: beginner Read time: ~10 min Prerequisites: Overfitting, underfitting, and reading a loss curve Verified: 13 Nov 2026

    Training produces a model; evaluation tells you whether it's any good. This lesson closes the core loop of Track 1: a fine-tune isn't finished when the loss flattens — it's finished when a metric on the gold set clears a bar you set in advance.

    Pick a metric that fits the shape

    From the task-shapes lesson: the metric must match the shape, or the number is meaningless. Quick map:

    • Classification → accuracy, and per-class precision / recall / F1 (plus a confusion matrix to see which classes confuse).
    • Extraction / NER → span-set precision/recall/F1 on exact (type, span) matches.
    • QA → exact-match / F1 against references, or an LLM judge for open answers.
    • Summarization → ROUGE for overlap plus a faithfulness check.
    • Structured output → valid-format rate + per-field correctness.

    A word on precision vs recall, since they recur everywhere: precision is "of what the model flagged, how much was right"; recall is "of what it should have found, how much it caught." F1 is their harmonic mean — one number when you care about both. Which matters more is a product decision (a PII detector usually prizes recall; a spam filter, precision).

    Always compare to a baseline

    A number alone is not evidence. "Is it better than what?" Evaluate the base model (before fine-tuning) on the same gold set, with the same prompt template and decoding settings, and report the fine-tuned model's score next to it. The lift over baseline is the thing your training actually bought. Other useful baselines: a simple prompt on a larger model, or the previous deployed version.

    Gates: decide the bar in advance

    A quality gate is a threshold you commit to before seeing the result ("ship only if gold-set F1 ≥ 0.85 and no safety regressions"). Setting it in advance stops you from rationalizing a mediocre model after the fact. Gates turn evaluation from a vibe into a decision rule.

    Is the difference real?

    A gold set is a sample, so every score carries noise. At 80% accuracy the 95% confidence interval is about ±11 points on 50 rows, ±8 on 100 and ±4.5 on 300 — a 4-point gap on 50 rows tells you almost nothing. A lift is only evidence when it's well outside the noise of the difference, roughly two standard errors. The box below shows the sharper test, comparing both models row by row, and the habits that keep a small test set honest.

    Small test sets: is the difference real?

    Score both models on the same rows and look at the change row by row (a paired comparison), not just at the two headline numbers. On a small test set one answer moves the score a lot: one row in 20 is 5 points, one in 50 is 2.

    BrewSLM pairs the rows, counts how many got better, worse or stayed the same, and puts a 95% confidence interval (a paired t-interval) around the mean change. If the interval includes zero, the change is within noise: the data cannot tell a gain from a loss. Under 5 paired rows it gives no verdict.

    Worked example: 50 test rows
    Base model22 right (44%)
    Fine-tuned26 right (52%): +8 points
    Row by row6 better, 2 worse, 42 the same
    95% interval−3 to +19 points: within noise
    Visible gapabout 16 points at this size; about 500 rows to see a 5-point change

    Habits that keep a small test honest:

    • Compare like with like: same rows, same answer key, same scoring and decoding settings. BrewSLM's Compare gives no verdict when the answer key, judge or scoring differ.
    • Practice, then final: iterate against the practice answer key and score the final one rarely. A set you consult on every decision ends up fitted to your choices.
    • Small slices are noise: a per-class or per-entity score on a handful of rows swings on one row. Show the row count next to it.
    • Seeds: two or three training seeds show how much runs vary; with that few the interval is wide, so read the spread as a rough sign of the noise, not as a test.

    Further reading: Evan Miller, "Adding Error Bars to Evals" (arXiv 2411.00640).

    Honest reporting (the rule that matters most)

    Report where the model loses, not just where it wins. Show the failing class, the slice with low recall, the examples it gets wrong. An evaluation that only surfaces good news is worse than none — it builds false confidence. The point of measuring is to find what to fix next.

    Evaluate on the gold set, then iterate

    Run the metric on the held-out gold set (never the training data), read the failures, and feed them back into the data-centric loop (Lesson 0.11): the classes and slices where the model loses tell you exactly which examples to add or fix before the next run.

    That completes the core loop of Track 1: objectives, data, the loss mask and chat templates, the training loop and its loss, learning rate and batch, LoRA and memory, and how to read and evaluate the result. The four lessons of 1C · Beyond the core loop come next — decoding controls, dataset formats, continued pretraining and catastrophic forgetting — and then Track 2, where you'll do all of it by hand in PyTorch and Transformers.

    Key terms

    Evaluation metric
    A shape-appropriate measure of quality (accuracy/F1, span-set F1, ROUGE + faithfulness, etc.).
    Precision / recall / F1
    Of flagged, how much right / of what should be found, how much caught / their harmonic mean.
    Baseline
    A reference score (base model, prompt, or previous version) the fine-tune is compared against.
    Quality gate
    A pass threshold set in advance that a model must clear to ship.
    Honest reporting
    Surfacing where the model loses, not only where it wins, to guide the next iteration.
